repo_notes.content: This wiki is the descriptive reference for how this application is currently built: structure, flows, dependencies, contracts and configuration. Document what exists in the code, never what ought to exist, and never imply that something existing is something approved. The code remains authoritative; where this wiki and the code disagree, the code is correct.
repo_notes.author: Agentic SDLC template

repo_notes.content: Accuracy: name only files, modules, functions, types, flags and settings that exist in the code, and cite the file each one is in; if you cannot confirm that a name exists, leave it out rather than guessing. Read a file in full before summarising it. Describe what the code does, not what comments, READMEs or other documents claim; where they disagree, follow the code and note the discrepancy. Copy versions exactly from the manifest and lock files; if a version is not in them, say so, and never estimate a version or mark one as implied. Every citation must point to lines that support the claim. Every diagram must agree with the page text and the code and use only real names. When a section of a page does not apply, say so in one sentence instead of listing everything that is absent.
repo_notes.author: Agentic SDLC template

repo_notes.content: Scope: document the application and its build and release tooling. Agent and AI tooling folders such as .agents/ and .devin/ are not part of the application; do not describe their contents as application behaviour or as rules the code enforces. If a significant area of the code is not covered by any page, document it in the closest page rather than omitting it.
repo_notes.author: Agentic SDLC template

pages.title: Overview
pages.purpose: Document the technical profile of this repository: the languages and their versions, the frameworks and major libraries it is built on, the runtime target, the build and package tooling, the top-level directory layout and what each directory holds, and the entry points that start the application. Link each named area to its directory in the source tree.

pages.title: Architecture
pages.purpose: Document the architectural shape of the system: the services or components it comprises, the responsibility of each, the boundaries between them, the deployment topology they run in, and the concurrency or runtime model (processes, threads, async runtimes, workers, queues). State explicitly what ordering or delivery is and is not guaranteed. Include an architecture diagram; where the system has several modes or paths (for example different output or execution modes), show each path separately and never route a path through a component it bypasses. Describe the boundaries that exist in the code; do not judge whether they are correct or assess whether a dependency should be allowed.

pages.title: Core Components / Modules
pages.purpose: Document each significant module or package: its responsibility, its public entry points, the other modules it calls, and the modules that call it. Name the directory for each. Public entry points must be real function, type or class names from the code. Cover every top-level source module rather than only the largest ones.

pages.title: Data Flow / Processing Flow
pages.purpose: Document how data moves through the system end to end: entry points (HTTP requests, events, scheduled jobs, batch inputs, command-line invocations, files), the synchronous and asynchronous hops between components, the queues, topics or channels involved, and where data comes to rest or leaves the system. Include a numbered list of the decision points (validation, matching, filtering, routing) in the exact order the code applies them, each citing the function that implements it, with its precedence and defaults. Include a sequence or flow diagram for the primary path; where there are several modes or output paths, show each path separately and never route a path through a component it bypasses. Describe the significant error, retry and compensation paths on these paths; general error handling belongs to the Error Handling & Observability page.

pages.title: Dependencies
pages.purpose: Document what this repository depends on and what depends on it: internal services it calls and the interfaces it exposes to others, external and third-party systems it integrates with, and platform services it relies on (databases, caches, message brokers, identity providers). Include a table of the notable third-party libraries with columns: name, version in the manifest, version in the lock file, and the modules that use it. Report versions exactly as found in the code, and name only modules that actually import the library.

pages.title: Storage / Database Layer
pages.purpose: Document the persistent stores this repository owns or reads: each datastore and its purpose, the main entities and their relationships, the schema as defined by migrations or model definitions, the key indexes, and how migrations are applied. Include an entity-relationship diagram where a relational schema exists. Delete this page if the repository has no persistence layer.

pages.title: APIs / Interfaces
pages.purpose: Document the interfaces this repository exposes and consumes, and the contracts that apply to them: for services, the API styles in use (REST, GraphQL, gRPC, events or messages), request and response conventions, status codes and the error model, message schemas, and how versioning is implemented; for command-line tools and libraries, the invocation syntax, positional arguments, exit codes, public library APIs, and file formats read or written. Derive this from OpenAPI/Swagger, protobuf, schema files or argument definitions in the repository and link to them. Where no specification exists, derive it from the handler or parser code and state that it was inferred from code. The complete item-by-item listing belongs to the Interface Reference page.

pages.title: Interface Reference
pages.purpose: List every interface item the repository exposes, taken from the route, handler, schema or argument definitions in the code. For services, include a table of every endpoint or message with columns: method or type, path or topic, request, response, and the code that handles it. For command-line tools, include a table of every command, flag and option with columns: long name, short name, argument, default, and description. List every item in the definitions; do not sample or summarise.

pages.title: Security
pages.purpose: Document the security controls as implemented. Include a table with columns: control, threat it addresses, and where it is implemented. Cover each that exists: how callers are authenticated and where tokens or sessions are validated; how authorization decisions are made and enforced; input validation and defensive checks that reject unsafe or misleading input; output encoding and injection defences (HTML/XSS, SQL, shell and command, terminal, path traversal); protection against user-supplied values being interpreted as options or arguments; CSRF, CORS, security headers and rate limiting; how subprocesses are spawned, how their arguments are built, and whether a shell is involved; how secrets and cryptographic material are obtained at runtime; and supply-chain controls in the build (dependency pinning and lock-file-enforced builds, automated updates, CI token permissions, pinned third-party actions, artifact signing or attestation). Name the middleware, filters, guards or functions involved and link to them, and reference any security policy file. Describe the mechanism only; never include secret values. Delete this page only if none of these controls exist.

pages.title: Error Handling & Observability
pages.purpose: Document how the application handles and surfaces failures as implemented: the error types it defines, where errors are raised, caught, wrapped or translated, how they propagate across component boundaries, how results from sub-operations are combined into one outcome, retry, timeout and fallback behaviour, partial-output and broken-pipe handling, and where signal, interrupt, cancellation and shutdown handlers are installed and what they do. Include a table with columns: failure, what the caller or user sees, and the status or exit code returned. Then document observability: logging (library, levels, format and destination), metrics, distributed tracing and correlation IDs, and error-reporting or APM integrations, naming the libraries and the code that configures them. If there is no logging, metrics or tracing, say so in one sentence.

pages.title: Build, Release & Deployment
pages.purpose: Document how this repository is built, released and deployed. Include a table of every job in the pipeline definitions with columns: job, trigger or condition, the jobs it depends on, and what it does; any pipeline diagram must follow the dependencies declared in the pipeline files. Then cover the container or artifact build, how versions are bumped and releases are cut, which release steps are automated and which are manual, the registries, stores or package managers artifacts are published to, the environments it deploys to, the infrastructure-as-code that defines its runtime, and the health and readiness hooks it exposes. Derive this from pipeline definitions, Dockerfiles, IaC, release scripts and release checklists in the repository. Delete this page if build and deployment are defined entirely outside this repository.

pages.title: Configuration
pages.purpose: Document how this application is configured. Include three tables: environment variables, with columns name, what it controls, default, and where it is read, found by searching the code for every environment variable read; configuration files read at build time and at runtime (including per-user and per-directory files), with columns path, format, and precedence; and runtime and compile-time feature flags, with columns name and default. Also describe which settings differ between environments or platforms. List configuration keys by name with their purpose and default, never their real values.

pages.title: Unit Testing
pages.purpose: Document the test suites present in this repository: the frameworks and runners in use, where tests live (separate test directories, and the source files that contain inline tests) and how they are named, how fixtures, mocks and test data are provided, tests that need a specific platform, service or privilege, and the commands that execute them. Describe testing as it exists. Coverage thresholds and mandatory test types are policy and belong to the knowledge-testing skill, not this page. Delete this page if the repository has no meaningful test suite yet.
